title: Fed Decision in September?
description:
The FED interest rates are defined in this market by the upper bound of the target federal funds range. The decisions on the target federal funds range are made by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings.

This market will resolve to the amount of basis points the upper bound of the target federal funds rate is changed by versus the level it was prior to the Federal Reserve's September 2026 meeting.

If the target federal funds rate is changed to a level not expressed in the displayed options, the change will be rounded up to the nearest 25 and will resolve to the relevant bracket. (e.g. if there's a cut/increase of 12.5 bps it will be considered to be 25 bps)

The resolution source for this market is the FOMC’s statement after its meeting scheduled for September 15-16, 2026 according to the official calendar: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm.

The level and change of the target federal funds rate is also published at the official website of the Federal Reserve at https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm.

This market may resolve as soon as the FOMC’s statement for their September meeting with relevant data is issued. If no statement is released by the end date of the next scheduled meeting, this market will resolve to the "No change" bracket.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves based on the official Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) statement issued after the September 15-16, 2026, meeting. The metric is the upper bound of the target federal funds range, measured by the change in basis points from the pre-September meeting level (currently 3.75%). The upper bound is precisely defined; if the rate changes to a level not listed in the options, it is rounded up to the nearest 25 bps. The official resolution source is the Federal Reserve's monetary policy calendar and open market operations page.

## Source History & Current Reading

As of July 26, 2026, the federal funds rate upper bound stands at 3.75% (target range 3.50–3.75%), established on December 11, 2025. No rate changes have occurred during 2026, with the FOMC holding the rate steady at every scheduled meeting (January 28, March 18, April 29, and June 17, 2026). The Federal Reserve's official open market operations page lists no changes since the December 12, 2025 update.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-15**: Fed officials expressed concerns about persistent inflation above the 2% target despite core CPI cooling, signaling a continued data-dependent, no-forward-guidance approach for the September meeting.
- **2026-07-08**: June 17 FOMC meeting minutes were published, revealing a split committee: half of the 18 policymakers favored unchanged or lower rates by year-end, while half favored increasing rates.
- **2026-07-01**: Chair Kevin Warsh stated at the ECB Forum that 'prices are too high' and emphasized his intent to avoid traditional forward guidance to prevent confirmation bias.
- **2026-06-17**: The FOMC voted 12-0 to hold the federal funds rate at 3.50–3.75%. The meeting's dot plot indicated 9 of 18 members project at least one hike before year-end.

## Key Factors

### 1. Inflation Trajectory _(uncertain)_

June 2026 CPI data show headline inflation at 3.5% and core CPI at 2.6% year-over-year. While core inflation decelerated from 2.9% in May, it remains above the 2% target. Fed officials treat the recent headline decline (aided by a 5.7% drop in energy prices) cautiously, focusing on core/services persistence. The current data reduces the immediate necessity for tightening while simultaneously failing to provide a clear justification for easing, forcing a holding pattern until further trends appear.

### 2. Labor Market Conditions _(uncertain)_

Nonfarm payroll growth slowed to 57,000 in June 2026, with significant downward revisions to April and May data. The unemployment rate is 4.2%, and labor force participation fell to 61.5%. While these figures reflect a 'cooling' market, layoffs remain low (215,000 initial claims) and the labor market is generally viewed as resilient enough to support economic expansion without immediate emergency rate cuts. The current status suggests moderate slack that does not yet force a dovish policy shift.

### 3. Fed Policy Stance and Communications _(uncertain)_

Under Chair Kevin Warsh, the FOMC has explicitly abandoned traditional forward guidance, preferring a data-driven approach that avoids pre-commitment. With the 18-member committee evenly split in June between hiking and holding/cutting, there is no unified consensus. The committee's primary focus remains on price stability, with officials signaling they are prepared to tighten if inflation prints 'hot', leaving the September decision highly sensitive to the upcoming August data cycle.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

CME FedWatch data (as of July 26, 2026) for the September 16, 2026 meeting reflects the following distribution: 17.8% probability for no change (3.50-3.75%), 57.3% for a 25 bps increase (3.75-4.00%), and 25.0% for a 50 bps increase (4.00-4.25%). The probability for any rate cut is currently 0%. Historically, rate moves usually occur in discrete 25 or 50 bp increments, though recent 2026 meetings have consistently resulted in 'no change'.

## Bottom Line

The resolution of this market depends on whether incoming inflation and employment data between July and August 2026 force the FOMC to break its current deadlock. The committee is split, and guidance has been explicitly minimized. The primary uncertainty is whether inflation remains 'sticky' above 2%, which would likely trigger a hike given the hawkish segment of the committee, or whether further slowing in payrolls/inflation cools the committee's enthusiasm for restriction. No cut is currently priced into market sentiment.

title: Strait of Hormuz traffic returns to normal by September 30?
description:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if IMF Portwatch publishes a 7-day moving average of transit calls (“Arrivals of Ships”) for the Strait of Hormuz equal to or above 60 for any date between market creation and September 30, 2026. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

Daily transit calls include container, dry bulk, roll-on/roll-off, general cargo, and tanker ships. Ships not reported by IMF Portwatch will not be considered.

This market will resolve as soon as IMF Portwatch publishes a 7-day moving average of transit calls equal to or above the specified level, or once data has been published for the final date in the specified period and no such value has been published. If no data has been published for the final date of the specified period within 14 calendar days (ET) after the end of that period, this market will resolve based on data published up to that point.

Revisions to previously published data points made within this market’s timeframe will be considered. However, they will not disqualify a previously published data point from qualifying. Revisions to previously published data points after data is published for September 30, 2026, however, will not be considered.

In case of obvious data integrity issues (i.e., erroneous data), the market may remain open until the end of the third calendar day (ET) after the date on which such data is first released to allow for corrections. Data integrity issues refer only to clerical or other similar errors in the underlying data, and do not include cases where IMF Portwatch differs from alternative sources.

The resolution source for this market will be IMF Portwatch, specifically the transit calls data published for the Strait of Hormuz at https://portwatch.imf.org/pages/cb5856222a5b4105adc6ee7e880a1730, both in the chart and through downloadable files.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

The market resolves to 'Yes' if the IMF PortWatch 7-day moving average (7DMA) of transit calls ('Arrivals of Ships') for the Strait of Hormuz is equal to or above 60 for any single date between July 2, 2026, and September 30, 2026. The metric relies on the daily volume of container, dry bulk, roll-on/roll-off, general cargo, and tanker ships. As of the latest data (2026-07-19), the 7DMA is 12.1, which is 47.9 units below the 60-ship threshold. The source is the IMF PortWatch ArcGIS dataset.

## Source History & Current Reading

The most recent verified data from IMF PortWatch (as of 2026-07-26, covering data up to 2026-07-19) shows a 7-day moving average of 12.1 transit calls per day. Daily totals over the last 7 days of available data (2026-07-13 to 2026-07-19) were 9, 6, 11, 12, 11, 10, 17, and 15, respectively. The highest 7-day moving average reported in the 30 days preceding July 26, 2026, was 33.9.

## Verified Source Data

**IMF PortWatch — Strait of Hormuz** (verified; fetched from the resolution source's ArcGIS data on 2026-07-26)

Metric: daily transit calls ("Arrivals of Ships"), by ship type. Data is satellite-derived and published with a processing lag (typically a few days), so the latest date below trails today.

- Latest available date: 2026-07-19

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-24**: Reuters cited Kpler data showing only one tanker crossing on July 23, the lowest level since May 7, amid rising war risks and oil prices hitting $100 per barrel.
- **2026-07-21**: Lloyd's List Intelligence reported that non-Iranian ship transits through the Strait plummeted 90% year-on-year, with tanker transits falling from 85 to 39 in one week.
- **2026-07-13**: Following the revocation of a sanctions waiver on Iranian oil on July 7, Trump announced the reinstatement of a naval blockade at Iranian ports and a 20% maritime toll on all cargo shipped through Hormuz.
- **2026-06-26**: The UN International Maritime Organization (IMO) paused evacuation plans for roughly 600 ships and 11,000 seafarers after an IRGC-led strike hit a vessel near Oman.
- **2026-06-17**: The U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to reopen the Strait via two corridors, initially resulting in a temporary spike in daily traffic (reaching 78 transits by June 25).

## Key Factors

### 1. Geopolitical Conflict and Security Risk _(lowers)_

The Strait remains a flashpoint for military escalation; recent attacks on ships (e.g., June 25 projectile strike and July 23 incidents) and the threat of naval blockades explicitly discourage commercial transit. Even when transit corridors are 'open,' security premiums and physical risks keep traffic significantly curtailed compared to pre-war norms.

### 2. Regulatory and Bureaucratic Hurdles _(lowers)_

Iran has increasingly asserted control over transit via the Revolutionary Guard-linked Persian Gulf Strait Authority, requiring transit permits and restricting passage to specific routes. The imposition of a new 20% maritime toll and competing navigational requirements from U.S. forces vs. Iranian forces increase the complexity and risk for ship operators, keeping volume below the threshold.

### 3. Global Oil Demand and Production _(uncertain)_

While the IEA forecasts a recovery in oil demand (noting a 6.5 mb/d increase in Gulf oil exports in June 2026 compared to May), this remains below pre-war averages. While theoretically positive for shipping volumes, the realized benefit is bottlenecked by the persistent security situation on the water, keeping the output-driven 'pull factor' for increased transits decoupled from actual vessel counts.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

In pre-crisis years (e.g., 2025), the 7-day moving average typically hovered between 80 and 100 ships per day, with an average of 93.7 across 2025. A 7-day moving average of 60 would represent a 'depressed' level relative to the 2025 historical baseline, meaning the market is not asking for a return to full peacetime volume, but rather a recovery to roughly 65% of normal activity levels.

## Bottom Line

The market requires a sustained 7-day moving average of 60 transit calls. Current activity (12.1) is approximately 80% below the required threshold. To reach 60, total daily traffic must increase by nearly 5x the current baseline. The outcome is highly sensitive to de-escalation of the U.S.-Iran conflict, specifically the lifting of the reported 20% toll, the cessation of maritime attacks, and the removal of the reported naval blockade, as these variables currently dictate shipowner willingness to use the Strait.

title: Maduro Prison Time?
description:
Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro was indicted in the Southern District of New York on January 3, 2026 on charges including Narco-Terrorism Conspiracy and Cocaine Importation Conspiracy. Maduro was indicted alongside alleged co-conspirators in an indictment titled "United States of America V. Nicolás Maduro Moros, Diosdado Cabello Rondón, Ramón Rodríguez Chacín, Cilia Adela Flores de Maduro, Nicolás Ernesto Maduro Guerra".

This market will resolve according to the prison sentence, if any, imposed on Nicolas Maduro (Nicolas Maduro Moros) relating to this indictment by December 31, 2027, 11:59 PM ET.

This market will resolve immediately based on the first sentence rendered in this case, regardless of any appeals. If Maduro is found not guilty, there is a mistrial, or if the first sentencing does not include any jail or prison time, this market will resolve to "No Prison Time."

If no sentencing takes place by December 31, 2027, 11:59 PM ET, this market will also resolve to "No Prison Time."

If Maduro is sentenced to life imprisonment without a specified numerical term of years, this market will resolve to the highest range bracket.

If the imposed sentence falls exactly between two brackets, this market will resolve to the higher range bracket.

For the purposes of this market, it does not matter whether the sentence is concurrent or consecutive to any existing sentence Maduro is already serving. The market will resolve based on the total prison sentence imposed in the first sentencing for this case.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the United States court system or other involved U.S. government sources; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

# Deep Research Report

## Resolution Mechanics

This market resolves based on the first sentencing delivered in the Southern District of New York regarding the criminal charges against Nicolás Maduro (including Narco-Terrorism Conspiracy and Cocaine Importation Conspiracy) provided by December 31, 2027, 11:59 PM ET. If no sentencing occurs by this deadline, if the defendant is acquitted, or if the court imposes no prison time, the market resolves to 'No Prison Time.' The primary resolution source is official documentation from the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York or consensus credible news reporting.

## Source History & Current Reading

On January 3, 2026, Nicolás Maduro was indicted in the Southern District of New York on counts of narcoterrorism conspiracy and cocaine importation conspiracy. Following his capture and detention, U.S. District Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein set a trial start date of June 1, 2027. Under the court's July 22, 2026, order, a detailed procedural calendar was established, including key pretrial deadlines extending into early 2027 (e.g., March 11, 2027 for final pretrial motions). Maduro remains in U.S. federal custody as of July 2026.

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2027-06-01**: Scheduled start date for the criminal trial of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.
- **2026-07-22**: Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein officially sets the trial start date for June 1, 2027, and establishes a procedural calendar for discovery and motion filings.
- **2026-04-01**: U.S. government modifies sanctions to allow the Venezuelan government to fund legal fees for Maduro, addressing a conflict of interest barrier.
- **2026-03-05**: The United States and Venezuela restore diplomatic and consular relations; the White House officially recognizes Delcy Rodríguez, not Maduro, as the leader of Venezuela.
- **2026-01-03**: Nicolás Maduro is indicted in SDNY on narco-terrorism and drug-trafficking charges; he is captured following a U.S. military-assisted operation in Caracas.

## Key Factors

### 1. Procedural Schedule and Sentencing Window _(uncertain)_

The critical factor for a timely resolution is the compressed timeframe between the set trial date of June 1, 2027, and the market deadline of December 31, 2027. Typical complex federal conspiracy cases often feature a trial length of 2 to 3 months followed by a post-verdict sentencing interval of 75 to 90 days. If the June 1, 2027, trial date holds, a verdict could reach the court by August or September 2027, leaving sufficient time for sentencing within the 7-month window by late 2027. However, systemic delays or procedural complexities regarding classified evidence discovery—scheduled for completion by November 15, 2026—could shift the trial, though the current schedule is explicitly characterized as 'realistic' by both prosecution and defense counsel.

### 2. Immunity and Legal Strategy _(uncertain)_

The defense's core strategy, articulated by lead attorney Barry Pollack, relies on asserting sovereign head-of-state immunity. The court has scheduled formal arguments on dismissal motions for November 17, 2026, following a first-round filing deadline of September 2, 2026. This legal challenge represents the most significant procedural obstacle to reaching a sentencing phase; if the defense successfully litigates these motions to a point of dismissing the charges or triggering interlocutory appeals that stall the schedule, the case could extend beyond the 2027 year-end deadline. Conversely, the U.S. Department of Justice maintains that the capture in Caracas was lawful per Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) opinions, and the lack of diplomatic recognition of Maduro by the White House limits the viability of the sovereign immunity defense.

### 3. Diplomatic Recognition and Political Climate _(raises)_

The shift in diplomatic recognition toward Delcy Rodríguez as the 'sole leader' of Venezuela significantly weakens Maduro’s arguments for incumbent head-of-state diplomatic immunity. While the Maduro defense is partially funded via a sanctioned government under an April 2026 U.S. waiver, the overall lack of aggressive state-level diplomatic friction over the trial—combined with the Rodríguez government’s focus on energy sector cooperation and eased oil sanctions—suggests the administration of the case is proceeding with limited high-level foreign intervention. This political climate reduces the pressure for diplomatic deals that might halt the trial, favoring the continued, standard progression of the judiciary schedule.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

The 2006 narcoterrorism statute (21 U.S.C. §960a) has resulted in only 83 charges in 20 years, with relatively few cases proceeding through full trial. Historical data shows that convictions on this count, when combined with large-scale cocaine importation (21 U.S.C. §§959, 960, 963), almost invariably result in multi-decade prison sentences due to federal sentencing guidelines (USSG §2D1.1 and §3A1.4) which impose heavy terrorism enhancements and categorize defendants into the highest criminal history brackets. Cases that avoid 'No Prison Time' historically trend toward the 20-to-life range, while 'No Prison Time' usually arises only from acquittals or mistrials, which occur rarely compared to plea-based conviction outcomes.

## Bottom Line

The resolution of this market entirely depends on whether the June 1, 2027, trial date proceeds without significant delay and whether the court can accommodate a verdict and subsequent sentencing hearing within the 7-month period remaining before the December 31, 2027, cutoff. While the legal complexity of a head-of-state immunity defense and classified evidence review presents significant friction, the established procedural calendar and the U.S. government's firm commitment to prosecuting the case under the current administration's diplomatic standing provide an infrastructure where sentencing is within the reach of the 2027 deadline.

As of July 26, 2026, Putin remains President, evidenced by active chairing of meetings and international diplomacy; the current state is 'No'.

## Source History & Current Reading

Latest state indicators: July 22, 2026 Kremlin transcript shows Putin actively managing Federal economy (June 2026 budget surplus of 196 billion rubles, GDP growth 0.3% in May 2026). ISW reports net territorial gain in Ukraine in H1 2026 of 97 km². VTsIOM polling for June 29–July 5, 2026 registers Putin's approval at 66.0% and trust at 72.3%, down from mid-June levels (70.4% approval, 76.7% trust).

## Recent Developments (dated)

- **2026-07-25**: Putin holds forum in Omsk; Kazakh President Tokayev publicly urges freezing Ukraine war; Putin responds by reaffirming war goals.
- **2026-07-23**: Kremlin confirms Putin to address State Duma on July 27 regarding the conclusion of the 8th convocation.
- **2026-07-22**: Official meeting chaired by Putin on economic issues is transcribed by the Kremlin, discussing monetary supply growth of 13% and regional budget loan extensions.
- **2026-07-09**: Reuters reports Putin rejects peace talk proposals from internal advisers and insists on escalation.
- **2026-06-25**: Reuters Breakingviews analyzes Russia's economic stagnation driven by defense spending, noting technocrat warnings to Putin regarding budget rules.

## Key Factors

### 1. Domestic Popular Legitimacy _(raises)_

Putin's approval has trended downward since mid-March 2026. VTsIOM data from late June/early July 2026 shows approval at 66.0% and trust at 72.3%, down from over 70% and 76% respectively in mid-June. This decline correlates with tangible economic impact, including a nationwide fuel shortage affecting at least 17 regions, high inflation (6% against a 4% target), and the extension of gasoline export bans until July 31, 2026. The shift from 'background' war to daily socio-economic friction (gas queues, inflation) directly challenges the regime's 'stability for control' contract.

### 2. Elite Cohesion and Institutional Control _(lowers)_

The Kremlin maintains a 'fortress' posture utilizing preemptive repression. Institutional transitions remain orderly, with the 8th State Duma concluding its standard term and new elections planned for September 2026. While elite debate regarding war strategy exists, as seen in reported friction regarding peace settlements, there is no evidence of a centralized challenge or rupture in the security services (siloviki). The state manages dissent by excluding anti-war figures like Boris Nadezhdin and leveraging legal changes to bolster security, effectively containing internal opposition.

### 3. Military Performance and Escalation _(raises)_

The disconnect between maximalist war objectives and minimal battlefield results creates a credibility gap. Russia realized a net gain of only 97 km² of territory in H1 2026 while suffering casualty estimates as high as 1.4 million personnel cumulative since 2022 (CSIS). Despite these costs, Putin continues to reject diplomatic off-ramps. This persistence forces a binary choice between escalation—which risks regime health via unpopular mobilization or economic collapse—and the current steady attrition that continues to slowly erode domestic support.

## Base Rates & Reference Class

Over ~110 years of Russian/Soviet history, roughly 3 of 8 major conflict/crisis periods resulted in the removal of the head of state (1917, 1964, 1991). The regime remained intact across other high-intensity events (World War II, 1980s Afghan War, 1918-1922 Civil War). This suggests that while wartime crises create instability, they historically do not necessitate the removal of the supreme leader in most cases, except during systemic failure.

## Bottom Line

The primary risk for a 'Yes' resolution lies in the cumulative effect of economic strain—specifically the fuel crisis and inflation—eroding popular support to a level where the Kremlin's repressive apparatus loses efficacy. Key developments to monitor include official confirmation of new national mobilization, significant escalation in elite-level dissent, or documented fractures in the security services, none of which are evident as of July 26, 2026. Stability currently rests on the continuation of managed repressive control despite measurable declines in approval.
